name: Golem effect
statement: Low expectations held by a teacher or a manager are said to depress the performance of the people held in them, the negative mirror of the Pygmalion effect.
meaning: The claim is causal and it runs from an adult's low belief to a subordinate's measured output. Symmetry is the part that has to be argued rather than assumed. That raising expectations helps says nothing about whether lowering them hurts, and the two directions could differ in size, in mechanism or in sign. The name comes from Babad, Inbar and Rosenthal, who took it from Hebrew slang, where golem means oaf or fool, and from the Jewish legend of an animated being that turned monstrous. Two neighbouring entries carry the positive direction. Teacher expectations and pupil IQ belong to the Pygmalion effect, no. 9, whose own verdict is mixed. The general mechanism belongs to the self-fulfilling prophecy, no. 44. Neither of those pages is evidence for this one.

origin.who: Elisha Y. Babad, Jacinto Inbar and Robert Rosenthal
origin.where: Journal of Educational Psychology, volume 74, issue 4, pages 459-474
origin.note: The paper named the negative direction and separated it from the positive one, which it called Galatea. It also drew the distinction the entry turns on, between teachers susceptible to biasing information and teachers who are not.

evidence: Babad, Inbar and Rosenthal identified 26 student teachers as biased or unbiased by how far their scoring of drawings shifted when they were told the artist was a high-status or a low-status pupil. Three groups of pupils followed, 202 in all: a randomly assigned high-expectancy group, and high-potential and low-potential groups the teachers nominated themselves. High-bias teachers treated their nominated low-potential pupils badly while treating the randomly assigned group as well as their own high-potential nominees. Unbiased teachers treated all three groups alike. The abstract reports the strongest and most consistent Golem effects for behavioural signs of dogmatism, and says the pattern appeared in pupils' performance on specially designed tasks as well as in teachers' behaviour. It carries no statistic. The low-expectancy group was nominated rather than randomised, so the negative half of that design is quasi-experimental. Everything after it splits into three kinds. The first prevents low expectations instead of inducing them. Oz and Eden told squad leaders in a military unit that low physical-fitness scores do not predict later performance, and left control squad leaders to interpret the scores themselves; low scorers under the treated leaders improved more. Reynolds puts that design at 17 treatment squad leaders against 17 controls. Leung and Sy describe the same study without those numbers, call the men paratroopers, and say Oz and Eden labelled the procedure de-golemization. Davidson and Eden ran two field experiments in the same spirit among women leading disadvantaged women, telling experimental leaders their trainees had higher than usual potential. Their abstract reports the predicted effects in both, and presents them as the first experimental confirmations of self-fulfilling prophecy among women as leaders. Neither study lowered anybody's expectations. The second kind induces the low expectation directly and is rare. Reynolds had a course instructor divide each class at random, then told one support instructor her group had done well on a management-acumen test, told a second that hers had done badly, and told a third nothing. Neither the students nor the support instructors knew the split was random, and new support instructors were used each year across four years of collection, 2001 to 2004. The sample was 374 full-time undergraduates at one large university in the north-eastern United States. Cup data were available for 351 of them and pretest and posttest scores for 275. On the follow-up test of the same kind, scores fell in all three groups: by 0.36 points under positive expectations, by 1.05 in the control group and by 1.89 under negative expectations, from pretest means of 10.78, 10.81 and 10.83 in that order. Reynolds reports the control group's change as not significant. Regressing the change on the treatments gives an R-squared of .16, F = 8.38, df 2 and 272, p < .001. On a second and unrelated task, folding origami cups in five minutes, the negative group made 20.82 cups on average, the positive group 17.87 and the control group 23.70, with an R-squared of .11, F = 19.75, df 2 and 348, p < .001. The third kind is correlational. Leung and Sy surveyed 202 followers and 101 leaders in real workgroups. A group's negative view of what followers are like predicted lower follower self-efficacy, at an unstandardised coefficient of -0.27, p < 0.01.

examples.tag: The class written off in September
examples.text: A teacher decides a group is weak, sets it undemanding work, asks it fewer questions and waits less time for an answer. The results duly stay low. What moved first was the teaching, and the label looks accurate afterwards because of what it caused.

A manager forms a low opinion of a new hire within a fortnight, hands them routine tasks and stops inviting them to the meetings where the work is decided. Their output stays thin, which the manager reads as confirmation rather than as the result of the diet they were put on.

examples.tag: The player left on the bench
examples.text: A coach who thinks a squad member cannot handle a close game keeps them out of close games. Match sharpness needs matches, so the judgement quietly removes the conditions under which it could have been shown wrong.

replication.headline: One field study has now lowered expectations directly at work, and the effect held for half the workers and reversed for the other half.
replication.detail: Ma and Zhu ran three studies on underdog expectations in Chinese workplaces, and the third is the repeat that matters. At a warehouse logistics firm in Yiwu, Zhejiang, they screened 391 packers into 101 with fixed mindsets, 276 with growth mindsets and 14 undetermined. They took 100 of each, 52.00% women, mean age 34.4 years with a standard deviation of 9.63, and split them at random into two groups. The treated group was put beside the best sorting line and told at each pre-shift meeting that it was performing far worse than the strong group. The control group was left alone. Output was boxes packed, logged automatically by radio frequency and averaged over a six-day week. Among fixed-mindset workers the treated group packed 241.50 boxes against 251.60 in the control group, t = -3.48, p = 0.001, df = 98. Among growth-mindset workers the treated group packed 262.20 against 252.10, t = 3.37, p = 0.001, df = 98. The Golem direction held for one half of the sample and reversed for the other. The two questionnaire studies, 341 employees and then 650, found the same split. In the first, underdog expectations crossed with a fixed mindset predicted feedback avoidance at 0.21, p < 0.001, and crossed with a growth mindset predicted the wish to prove others wrong at 0.23, p < 0.01. The article is in Chinese. Its tables and test statistics were read directly, its prose through machine translation, so every figure here is language-independent and no quotation from it appears. The old absence claim on this page also failed against sources it already cited. Reynolds writes that Davidson and Eden replicated the Oz and Eden approach, and Davidson and Eden ran two field experiments, so one of the original authors repeated his own prevention design and got the predicted result twice. Nobody has repeated Babad, Inbar and Rosenthal. Nobody has repeated Reynolds's classroom induction, which he himself asked for. No meta-analysis of the Golem effect was found. Searched on 21 September 2026: Crossref by title and by each founding DOI, OpenAlex until its free daily budget ran out, Semantic Scholar citation lists for all four founding papers, Europe PMC, PubMed, Unpaywall and the open web. PsycNET served a bot challenge rather than a record. A PubMed title and abstract search that day for 'golem effect' or 'golem effects' returns three records in total, against 34 for the Pygmalion equivalent. One of the three is a 2026 narrative review of expectation effects in surgical training.

study.cite: Ma, J., & Zhu, M. (2023). Accept or change your fate: Exploring the Golem effect and underdog effect of underdog expectations. Acta Psychologica Sinica, 55(6), 1029-1048.

limits: The ethical obstacle is the whole shape of this literature. A study cannot randomly assign people to be thought stupid by their teacher or their commander, so almost every design either measures low expectations that arose on their own, or blocks them from forming and reads the effect off the untreated controls. Eden's review of field methods sets this out as a deliberate strategy, inverting a harmful treatment so that the harm shows up in the group that was left alone. It buys ethical clearance at a price: the control condition carries the effect, and nothing was manipulated in the direction the theory is about. Ma and Zhu's field study is the exception, and it lowered expectations at work for a week. Several papers here were not opened, and the reasons differ. Oz and Eden's paper and Davidson and Eden's are recorded as closed by Unpaywall and OpenAlex, with no repository copy anywhere; APA's PsycNET answered with a bot challenge on 21 September 2026 rather than a paywall notice. Davidson and Eden's abstract was read at PubMed. Oz and Eden's design is reported above only as Reynolds, Leung and Sy, and Eden's own 2017 review describe it, and no effect size from either study appears on this page. Babad, Inbar and Rosenthal's paper is also closed, and the account above comes from the abstract on the Hebrew University research record, which gives no statistics. Vrugt's paper is closed at Springer, and the University of Amsterdam repository record holds no file, only metadata and a link to the publisher. The abstract read there gives 18 beginning male therapists interviewing 18 male psychology students, after a preliminary study of 26 and 36, and its outcome is the interviewee's discomfort in filled pauses and speech disturbances rather than any measure of performance. Romney, Harrison and Benson's systematic review of self-fulfilling prophecy research, which searched Business Source Premier from January 2001 to October 2022 with 'Golem effect' among its four keywords, could not be opened either: Emerald returned a Cloudflare bot challenge with status 403, and only the structured abstract deposited at Crossref was read. No count of Golem studies from it appears here. Where the question has been asked in the reverse direction the answer has come back reversed. Nurmohamed reports across four studies that being seen as unlikely to succeed can raise performance, through the wish to prove others wrong, and that it lowers performance when the observers' expectations look credible. That abstract was read on his own research page; the article is closed and no figure from it appears here. Xue, Zhu, Guo and Kong surveyed 346 employees at five Shanghai firms in three waves, pairing leaders with employees, and found the same fork: an avoidance path at 0.090, p < 0.01, and a prove-others-wrong path at 0.189, p < 0.001. Their outcome is work engagement, not task performance. Ziegler, Broome and Heller studied 311 German grammar-school pupils and their parents before the pupils' first physics lessons, and call the harm done to girls by parents who see physics as a boys' subject a Golem effect. That paper is in German, only its abstract was read, and it carries no manipulation and no figure that could be used here.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat the Pygmalion literature as evidence for the Golem effect. It is not, and no amount of positive-expectancy data settles the negative side. Wikipedia's entry attributes to McNatt's meta-analysis the finding that Golem effects hold at about the same magnitude in the workplace; McNatt's subject was Pygmalion interventions. A second error runs the other way, treating the thin trial record as proof the effect is imaginary. Few people have looked, for a reason that has nothing to do with whether the effect is real. The third is to read Oz and Eden or Davidson and Eden as demonstrations that low expectations harm people. Both raised or protected expectations and inferred the harm from the group nobody protected. Reynolds's own numbers repay attention, and his table and his prose disagree. The table shows every group's mean falling between pretest and posttest, including the group told it was clever, which dropped 0.36 points; the text of the same paper says scores were significantly higher under positive treatment and that the control group did not change significantly. On the unrelated folding task the group told it was hopeless beat the group told it was clever, while the group told nothing beat them both. Ma and Zhu are read too quickly in the other direction. Their field experiment is not a clean confirmation of the Golem effect, because half their workers packed more boxes after being told they were falling behind, and the split was by a trait they had measured in advance.

sources.text: Babad, E. Y., Inbar, J., & Rosenthal, R. (1982). Pygmalion, Galatea, and the Golem: Investigations of biased and unbiased teachers. Journal of Educational Psychology, 74(4), 459-474. Closed access; the abstract was read on 21 September 2026 at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem research record, and gives no statistics.

Oz, S., & Eden, D. (1994). Restraining the Golem: Boosting performance by changing the interpretation of low scores. Journal of Applied Psychology, 79(5), 744-754. Not opened. Unpaywall and OpenAlex record it closed with no repository copy, and PsycNET answered a bot challenge on 21 September 2026. Design and result are reported above as Reynolds (2007), Leung and Sy (2018) and Eden (2017) describe them.

Davidson, O. B., & Eden, D. (2000). Remedial self-fulfilling prophecy: Two field experiments to prevent Golem effects among disadvantaged women. Journal of Applied Psychology, 85(3), 386-398. Full text closed; the abstract was read at PubMed on 21 September 2026, and is the source for the two experiments and for the statement that only one experiment had then demonstrated the Golem effect.

Reynolds, D. (2007). Restraining Golem and Harnessing Pygmalion in the Classroom: A Laboratory Study of Managerial Expectations and Task Design. Academy of Management Learning & Education, 6(4), 475-483. Full text read; all figures above come from its Table 1 and Results section.

Leung, A., & Sy, T. (2018). I Am as Incompetent as the Prototypical Group Member: An Investigation of Naturally Occurring Golem Effects in Work Groups. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 1581. Open access; full text read.

Eden, D. (2017). Field Experiments in Organizations. Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, 4, 91-122. Source for the argument that a harmful treatment can be studied by inverting it.

Nurmohamed, S. (2020). The Underdog Effect: When Low Expectations Increase Performance. Academy of Management Journal, 63(4), 1106-1133. Closed; the abstract was read on the author's own research page at profnurmo.com on 21 September 2026. No figure from it appears above.

Ma, J., & Zhu, M. (2023). Accept or change your fate: Exploring the Golem effect and underdog effect of underdog expectations. Acta Psychologica Sinica, 55(6), 1029-1048. Publisher PDF downloaded and read. The article is in Chinese; its tables and test statistics were read directly and its prose through machine translation.

Vrugt, A. (1990). Negative attitudes, nonverbal behavior and self-fulfilling prophecy in simulated therapy interviews. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 14(2), 77-86. Named by Reynolds as the only earlier direct test of negative expectations. Closed at the publisher; the University of Amsterdam repository record holds no file, and its abstract was read there on 21 September 2026.

Xue, J., Zhu, M., Guo, Y., & Kong, D. (2022). The Double-Edged Sword of Underdog Expectations in Organizations in Shanghai, China: The Mediating Role of Feedback-Avoiding Behaviors and Proving Others Wrong and the Moderating Role of Regulatory Focus. Psychology Research and Behavior Management, 15, 2205-2218. Open access; full text read.

Romney, A., Harrison, J. T., & Benson, S. (2023). Looking back to predict the future: a review of empirical support for the self-fulfilling prophecy. Management Research Review, 47(2), 245-260. Not opened; Emerald returned a bot challenge with status 403 on 21 September 2026 and Unpaywall records it closed. Only the structured abstract deposited at Crossref was read.

In German; only the abstract, deposited at Crossref, was read on 21 September 2026. No figure from it appears above.
